nodes.name: Ghost gum
nodes.desc: A eucalypt of open, grassy woodland. Its pale cream flowers appear around October to November and, as a Myrtaceae tree, offer nectar and pollen to birds and bats.

nodes.name: Fig trees
nodes.desc: Fig trees bear fruit that feeds many forest birds and fruit bats. Wikipedia lists figs among the main foods of the hooded pitohui and the spectacled flying fox.

nodes.name: Red grass
nodes.desc: A tussock grass of open savannah and woodland. Grasses like this cover the lower, drier slopes beside the rainforest.

nodes.name: Orange passion flower
nodes.desc: A passion-flower vine. GloBI records the eastern red lacewing butterfly feeding on it.

nodes.name: Gray dorcopsis
nodes.desc: A forest wallaby of southern New Guinea that lives in forest and disturbed ground such as old gardens. It browses vegetation.

nodes.name: Spectacled flying fox
nodes.desc: A large fruit bat. It eats rainforest fruit, especially figs, and eucalypt and other Myrtaceae flowers. It is the most recorded mammal in the GBIF circle.

nodes.name: Rainbow lorikeet
nodes.desc: A nectar and fruit feeder. Eucalypt nectar is an important food, and it also takes figs.

nodes.name: Raggiana bird-of-paradise
nodes.desc: The national bird of Papua New Guinea. It eats mainly fruit and arthropods and is an important seed disperser for some New Guinea trees.

nodes.name: Hooded pitohui
nodes.desc: Eats mostly fruit, especially figs, plus insects and other invertebrates. Its skin and feathers carry batrachotoxin, which may deter predators.

nodes.name: Eastern red lacewing
nodes.desc: A butterfly whose caterpillars feed on passion-flower vines. GloBI records it feeding on Passiflora aurantia.

nodes.name: Asian weaver ant
nodes.desc: Eats other insects and the honeydew of sap-sucking insects it tends. By deterring plant-eating insects it protects the trees it nests in.

nodes.name: Rainbow skink
nodes.desc: A small skink recorded often in the area and endemic to Papua New Guinea. Small lizards like this are prey for kookaburras, pythons and monitors.

nodes.name: Cane toad
nodes.desc: An introduced toad. Wikipedia says it was released in New Guinea in the 1930s. It eats many invertebrates, including ants, and is itself eaten by crows and kookaburras.

nodes.name: Blue-winged kookaburra
nodes.desc: Eats ground animals such as insects, lizards and frogs. GloBI records it eating cane toads.

nodes.name: Torresian crow
nodes.desc: An omnivore that eats invertebrates, fruit, carrion and smaller birds. GloBI records it eating cane toads, which it can kill safely.

nodes.name: Brahminy kite
nodes.desc: Mainly a scavenger of dead animals. It occasionally hunts live prey such as bats.

nodes.name: Green tree python
nodes.desc: Eats mainly small mammals, with some lizards. Wikipedia names green tree pythons as predators of birds in New Guinea.

nodes.name: Crocodile monitor
nodes.desc: A large tree-dwelling lizard that eats birds, small mammals, eggs, other reptiles, frogs and carrion.

nodes.name: Sunlight
nodes.desc: Strong tropical sunshine drives plant growth in both forest and savannah.

nodes.name: Seasonal rain
nodes.desc: Rain feeds the rainforest. The park mixes dense forest with drier open savannah, so the wet and dry seasons shape which plants grow where.

nodes.name: Soil nutrients
nodes.desc: Nutrients recycled from dead plants and animals feed the next growth of trees and grass.

nodes.name: Decomposers
nodes.desc: Fungi, bacteria and insects that break down dead leaves and carcasses and return nutrients to the soil.
